name: Congo-Brazzaville Poulet Moambe
description: Poulet moambe, chicken in a real palm-nut sauce, is widely considered Congo-Brazzaville's national dish, sharing its name and roots with the version found across the river in DR Congo - real moambe sauce is genuinely palm-fruit-based, not primarily peanut, though peanut butter is the recognized stand-in when palm nut cream isn't available.
steps_detailed: Brown the chicken with the onion and garlic in the palm oil, 8-9 minutes.
Whisk the peanut butter with the tomatoes and a little water, then add to the pot.
Simmer 25-28 minutes until the chicken is very tender.
steps: Brown the chicken with the onion and garlic in the palm oil, 8-9 minutes.
Whisk the peanut butter with the tomatoes and a little water, then add to the pot.
Simmer 25-28 minutes until the chicken is very tender.

name: Congo-Brazzaville Saka Saka
description: Saka saka, pounded cassava leaves cooked in real palm oil and peanut butter, is a beloved Congo-Brazzaville staple, its name literally being the Congolese word for cassava - real cassava leaves aren't a distinct item here, so spinach stands in for a milder approximation.
steps_detailed: Cook the onion and garlic in the palm oil, 3-4 minutes.
Add the spinach and a splash of water, cover, and simmer 15-18 minutes until well combined and tender.
Stir in the peanut butter and simmer uncovered 10 minutes more until thickened.
steps: Cook the onion and garlic in the palm oil, 3-4 minutes.

name: Congo-Brazzaville Madesu
description: Madesu, white beans stewed in real palm oil and tomato paste, is a genuine Congo-Brazzaville staple, real technique cooking the tomato paste until it deepens before the beans go in.

ingredients_full.ingredient: Cowpeas (blackeyes), immature seeds, cooked, boiled, drained, without salt

ingredients.ingredient: Cowpeas (blackeyes), immature seeds, cooked, boiled, drained, without salt

steps_detailed: Cook the onion in the palm oil, 3-4 minutes.
Add the tomato paste and cook 2 minutes until it deepens in color.
Add the cowpeas and a splash of water, and simmer 15-18 minutes until well combined.

name: Congo-Brazzaville Liboke
description: Liboke, fish or meat wrapped in banana leaf and steamed, is a beloved Congo-Brazzaville cooking method, real technique sealing in real steam and aroma that open cooking can't replicate.
steps_detailed: Rub the fish with the garlic and ginger.
Wrap tightly in foil (standing in for banana leaf) with the tomatoes.
Bake at 400F (200C) for 20-22 minutes until just cooked through, sealed in its own steam.
steps: Rub the fish with the garlic and ginger.

Bake at 400F (200C) for 20-22 minutes until just cooked through, sealed in its own steam.

name: Congo-Brazzaville Fufu
description: Fufu, cassava pounded into a smooth, stretchy dough, is one of Congo-Brazzaville's most essential staples, traditionally torn by hand to scoop up sauce.
steps_detailed: Boil the cassava until completely soft, 20-25 minutes.
Drain and pound vigorously until smooth and stretchy, free of lumps.
steps: Boil the cassava until completely soft, 20-25 minutes.
Drain and pound vigorously until smooth and stretchy, free of lumps.

name: Congo-Brazzaville Poulet Braisé (Grilled Chicken)
description: Poulet braisé, marinated grilled chicken, is a beloved Congo-Brazzaville dish, real technique marinating with garlic and ginger before the smoky char of the grill.
steps_detailed: Marinate the chicken in the garlic, ginger, and lemon juice for at least 20 minutes.
Grill, turning, 12-15 minutes, until charred and cooked through.
steps: Marinate the chicken in the garlic, ginger, and lemon juice for at least 20 minutes.
Grill, turning, 12-15 minutes, until charred and cooked through.

name: Congo-Brazzaville Peanut Soup
description: A rich peanut soup, popular especially in the coastal city of Pointe-Noire, real technique whisking the peanut butter slowly to keep the broth smooth.
steps_detailed: Cook the garlic in a little oil 30 seconds.
Whisk in the peanut butter and broth slowly, and simmer 12-15 minutes until smooth and lightly thickened.
steps: Cook the garlic in a little oil 30 seconds.
Whisk in the peanut butter and broth slowly, and simmer 12-15 minutes until smooth and lightly thickened.

name: Congo-Brazzaville Grilled Fish
description: Grilled fish rubbed with garlic and lemon, reflecting Congo-Brazzaville's real coastal and Congo River fishing tradition.
steps_detailed: Rub the fish with the garlic and lemon juice, and let sit 10 minutes.
Grill or broil, 4-5 minutes per side, until just cooked through.
steps: Rub the fish with the garlic and lemon juice, and let sit 10 minutes.

name: Congo-Brazzaville Fried Plantain
description: Fried ripe plantain, a common Congo-Brazzaville side dish, real versions using genuinely ripe plantain for real caramelization.
steps_detailed: Fry the plantain slices in a little oil, turning once, 3-4 minutes per side, until deeply caramelized and golden.

Add the carrot, potato, and tomatoes, and simmer 30-35 minutes until tender.

name: Congo-Brazzaville Peanut Sauce
description: A simple ground-peanut sauce base, echoing the flavor of moambe, used across many Congo-Brazzaville stews.
steps_detailed: Whisk the peanut butter slowly with 1 cup water and the tomatoes into a smooth sauce.
Simmer 12-15 minutes until thickened.
